For boards & managing agents

Local Law 11 / FISP, in plain English

New York’s Facade Inspection & Safety Program — FISP, still widely called Local Law 11 — requires the facades of buildings taller than six stories to be inspected up close by a licensed design professional (a QEWI) and filed with the Department of Buildings every five years. Miss the cycle or file late, and the fines start compounding.

Every filed facade lands in one of three categories:

SAFE
No repairs required

The facade needs no work this cycle. You file, you’re done until the next cycle.

SWARM
Safe, with repairs on a deadline

“Safe With a Repair and Maintenance Program” — the conditions noted must be corrected by the date in the report, or the facade is reclassified UNSAFE.

UNSAFE
Immediate action required

The building must protect the public — typically a sidewalk shed — and complete repairs on the city’s clock, not yours.

Where Zicklin comes in: your engineer inspects and files. We do the repair work itself — the probes, repointing, brick and lintel replacement the report calls for — priced in writing before we start.

  1. Send us the report. Your QEWI’s FISP filing or a managing agent’s repair list is enough to start.
  2. Site visit & probes. We confirm conditions on the wall, not from the sidewalk.
  3. Written estimate in 48 hours. Itemized by condition, so boards can approve line by line.
  4. Repairs & sign-off support. Work documented for your engineer’s amended filing.

Heritage

On New York walls since 1987

Thirty-seven-plus years of the same trade, in the same city. The laws changed, the scaffolding changed — the standard didn’t.

  1. 1987

    Founded in New York City

    Zicklin Contracting Corp. opens for business — a masonry-first contractor serving the city’s commercial and residential buildings.

  2. 1998

    The Local Law 11 era begins

    New York passes Local Law 11 of 1998, greatly expanding facade inspection requirements citywide. Facade repair becomes a core discipline — and stays one.

  3. 2000s

    The co-op & condo decades

    As pre-war co-ops and converted buildings across Manhattan and Brooklyn take on capital programs, the work follows: facades, parapets, waterproofing, and flat roofs, building by building.

  4. 2020

    FISP Cycle 9

    The inspection program is renamed the Facade Inspection & Safety Program (FISP) with tighter rules and closer-up inspections — more probes, more hands-on repair, more of exactly this work.

  5. Today

    Same trade, same standard

    Structural masonry, facade restoration, and flat roofing for co-ops and building owners — rated 4.9★ across 103 Google reviews, licensed by NYC DCA #2107837-DCA.
